source: Tsui et al. (2025) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot in LLMs
finding: Models fix an error when it is shown as coming from outside, but miss the same error in their own output. Reasoning models show almost no such gap.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-math (BIG-Bench Mistake logic and tracking) 62.8%. Appending 'Wait' after the error cut the blind spot 89.3% on average. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cut it 76.0%. Reasoning models: small, even negative blind spot.
limits: Errors are injected into the model's own output, not natural errors. Mostly math. Measures correcting a known-bad answer, not finding a bad one. Single preprint.
agent_relevance: Self-review is not dead for long-thinking models, but a non-reasoning base still needs a trigger. Test: a forced 'Wait'-style recheck on the committed diagnosis versus none, at equal tokens. Bears on gap 8.

source: Tsui et al. (2025) Self-Correction Bench, section 4.4 reasoning models
finding: Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning base model almost matches its reasoning sibling. The gap looks like trained habit, not capacity.
limits: Correction benchmark with injected errors, not equal-token cost; reasoning models use far more tokens. Not code debugging.
agent_relevance: A cheap correction marker may substitute for long thinking when the error is known to be in view. Does not show the agent can find the error without a signal.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Across the literature, self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists, not when the same prompted LLM gives the feedback. Many positive results used oracle information or weak baselines.
numbers: Three conclusions: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs outside tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) works well where reliable external feedback exists (code interpreters etc.); (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Covers papers to May 2024.
limits: Survey, papers up to May 2024; pre-dates current long-thinking models. Authors' judgement of fairness of each setup.
agent_relevance: Settles the 2023-24 picture for gap 3 and 8: the signal, not the reflection prompt, carries the gain. Use tools (run, test, trace) as the feedback source.

source: Gou et al. (2023) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Critique grounded in tools (interpreter, search) improves answers. The same critique loop without the tool is unstable and can hurt.
numbers: Math-program tasks: CRITIC w/o Tool changed text-davinci-003 by -1.8 points on one set; Self-Refine on Codex fell further. 2-3 correction rounds give most of the gain. Critique-conditioned regeneration beat rejection sampling by 4.5 and 3.3 EM on QA. Self-Eval verification of its own answers was 54% on HotpotQA, near chance.
limits: 2023 models (ChatGPT, text-davinci-003, LLaMA-2); tools are an interpreter and a search API, not a debugger. Gains larger with bigger models.
agent_relevance: Supports the cheap tool-grounded signal for gap 3: interpreter output is enough in program tasks. Does not compare against human feedback.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: An LLM that states a hypothesis, a prediction and a debugger experiment, then reads the real output, repairs bugs competitively. Real execution results make the agent's 'done' signal informative; imagined results make it misleading.
numbers: Repair competitive with Recoder and fine-tuned InCoder on Defects4J, ARHE, BugsInPy. With real debugger output, bugs with a DONE prediction were 12.4 points more likely to have a plausible patch. With LLM-hallucinated debugger output, DONE bugs were 11 points LESS likely. Human study, 20 participants (6 professionals): explanations raised accuracy in 5 of 6 real bugs at about the same time; only 1 of 6 professionals was satisfied.
limits: No ablation of one hypothesis versus three competing ones. Python and Java, small benchmarks. Hypothesis loop and debugger are confounded.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 2/3: the benefit sits in the observation step. It does not test the three-hypotheses-before-first-edit claim; gap 2 stays open.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents, patch validation ablation
finding: A fixed localize, repair, validate pipeline matched agents on SWE-bench Lite. Most of the late gain came from generated reproduction tests used to pick among candidate patches.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (300, GPT-4o): majority vote only 77 fixed (25.67%, $0.00); + regression tests 81 (27.00%, $0.01); + reproduction tests 96 (32.00%, $0.25). Average total cost $0.70. 40 patch samples; upper bound if all samples counted 126 (42.0%). One greedy reproduction test gave 90 fixes; 40 candidate tests gave 96.
limits: Selection among up to 40 samples, so it is not a reproduce-first agent. The +15 comes with sampling cost. Pipeline and agent differ in more than one way, so the pipeline vs open-choice contrast is still confounded.
agent_relevance: Reproduction as a selector helps (+15 fixes over regression-only). For gap 9, this is evidence for tests as the gate, not for removing agent choice.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless, reproduction test quality
finding: Most generated reproduction tests reproduce the symptom but do not correctly verify the fix. A wrong test is itself a wrong first hypothesis that is then trusted.
numbers: Of 300 issues, 213 reproduction tests reproduced the issue on the original repo; only 94 also printed 'Issue resolved' after the ground-truth patch. Pipeline falls back to regression tests when no patch passes.
limits: Test written from issue text only; ambiguity in the issue is the main cause per the authors.
agent_relevance: Cost of reproduce-first: a bad reproduction anchors the agent. The gate must be checked against a second signal.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces, failure modes of unresolved instances
finding: Most SWE-agent failures are a wrong or too-narrow fix, not a missed file. Failed edits cascade.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo on SWE-bench Lite, 248 unresolved runs, categorised by GPT-4o (87% agreement with authors on a validation set): 52.0% Incorrect or Overly Specific Implementation; 23.4% failed edit recovery; remaining categories under 25% combined.
limits: Automatic labels, 2024 model, categories chosen by authors, not a Ko-and-Myers coding of first wrong hypothesis. Does not say whether the first hypothesis was revisited.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: the dominant failure is a wrong fix after localisation, consistent with a bad diagnosis, but chain structure is not measured.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent, interface ablation and editing guardrail
finding: A tool gate that rejects a syntax-breaking edit and shows the error raised success; the same interface with no gate did worse. Early submits succeed more.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4 Turbo: edit with linting 18.0%; edit without linting 15.0% (-3.0); no edit tool 10.3% (-7.7). Viewer 30 lines 14.3, full file 12.7, 100 lines 18.0. 51.7% of 2,294 runs had at least one failed edit. Chance an edit eventually succeeds 90.5%, falling to 57.2% after one failed edit. Resolved runs median 12 steps, $1.21; unresolved mean 21 steps, $2.52. 93.0% of resolved runs submitted before budget exhaustion versus 69.0% overall.
limits: Single model, 300 tasks, +/- values are the paper's standard errors. Linting guards syntax, not 'is a change needed' (action bias).
agent_relevance: Evidence on gap 7: a tool-based gate that blocks bad edits works where a prompt cannot. Not tested for the is-a-change-needed gate. Also supports a step-count stop rule: long runs fail.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: A grounded-theory taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three groups. Verification failures are a large group, and the labelling is reliable enough to scale with an LLM judge.
numbers: 150 traces annotated by experts, Cohen's kappa 0.88 in final rounds; 1,600+ traces over 7 multi-agent systems; LLM annotator accuracy 94%, kappa 0.77. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 open MAS. Modes: wrong assumption without clarifying 6.8%; premature termination 6.2%; no or incomplete verification 8.2%; incorrect verification 9.1%; reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%. Fixing role authority in ChatDev gave +9.4% task success; the authors say such fixes are not enough.
limits: Multi-agent frameworks (ChatDev, MetaGPT, etc.), mostly small programming tasks with GPT-4o, not single-agent debugging. Not coded with Ko and Myers' scheme. Percentages are shares of annotated failure modes as reported in the paper's first table.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue to coding failures as a taxonomy: bad assumptions and bad verification are a visible share. Supports logging agent failures by type, but gives no root-then-chain fraction for gap 1.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? (Who&When)
finding: Locating the decisive error step in an agent log is hard for LLMs, with some methods below random.
numbers: 127 multi-agent systems. Best method: 53.5% agent accuracy, 14.2% step accuracy. GPT-4o with ground truth, algorithm-generated systems, step accuracy: random 19.06, all-at-once 12.50 (below random), step-by-step 25.51, binary search 23.98. Hand-crafted (Magentic-One) step accuracy only 5.26 to 7.02 versus random 4.16. Accuracy falls as context length grows. Hybrid (all-at-once to pick agent, then step-by-step) improved step accuracy at highest token cost. o1 and R1 also not practical.
limits: Multi-agent logs, not coding trajectories. Table columns were read from extracted text; the mapping of random-row values to columns is my reading.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a log-reading earliest-error detector is not reliable enough to trigger rollback on its own. Trigger on external signals (test results, diffs), not on an LLM reading the transcript.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search: MCTS and iterative refinement for software agents
finding: Giving the agent backtracking via tree search with an LLM value function raised resolve rate, but the value function is only fair at telling good branches from bad ones.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, five models: 23% average relative improvement over the base agent. Value function 73% accurate in solution evaluation; the debate discriminator raised final selection to 84%. Letting the plan state jump to any state without search added only 1.4%. Search costs more tokens.
limits: The compute-matched table (Pass@5) was garbled in extraction and not read cleanly. Value accuracy is on the authors' own set. Moatless base agent, not a long-thinking model.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: rollback with a learned value signal pays off in aggregate; free-form self-redirection alone barely does. A tool-grounded signal is not part of the value function.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The danger of overthinking: the reasoning-action dilemma in agentic tasks
finding: Reasoning models in SWE-bench agents often plan instead of acting. Higher overthinking scores go with lower resolve rates. Picking the least-overthinking run helps.
numbers: 4,018 trajectories on SWE-bench Verified; LLM-judge overthinking score agrees with human experts. Reasoning models score about 3 times higher than non-reasoning ones. Three patterns: analysis paralysis, rogue actions, premature disengagement. Selecting lowest overthinking of k=2 low-effort samples: 27.3% with 43% less cost; k=3: 30.3%, above the high-effort configuration with 15% less cost. o1 low effort scored 35% higher on overthinking than high.
limits: Early 2025 models; SWE-bench contamination applies. Correlation, plus a selection intervention, not an edit of the trace. Overthinking is the opposite pole of the action bias in K13.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and 8: current long-thinking models fail the opposite way to the 2023 action bias, by acting too little. Gate both ways: act on a real signal, not on inner simulation.

source: Mundler et al. (2024) SWT-Bench: testing and validating real-world bug fixes with code agents
finding: Reproduction tests made by an agent are a strong filter on fixes. Reproducing an issue and fixing it are different tasks per sample.
numbers: SWE-agent filtered by its own fail-to-pass tests: precision of accepted fixes 47.8% (more than double the unfiltered rate), recall about 20%. Giving the model the test files to change roughly doubled test success (8.1% to 15.1%); giving a golden patch raised it only to 10.5%. An ideal ensemble of the best four methods solved 71% more samples than the best single method.
limits: Python only; SWE-bench repos. Filter lowers recall, so the agent submits less. SWE-agent produces both test and fix, so the gain is a selection gain.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: test-as-gate improves precision, not total fixes. Together with Agentless, gains come from filtering, not from forbidding open choice.

source: Meng et al. (2024) An empirical study on LLM-based agents for automated bug fixing
finding: Across six top SWE-bench Verified systems, finding the right place matters, and a reproduction script unrelated to the fix can derail the run.
numbers: 500 instances: 96 not solved by any tool; 181 solved by all. Authors' own agent with Claude 3.5 Sonnet solved 255 (51%). Of 500 generated reproduction scripts, 384 (76.8%) changed status when the golden patch was applied. Related scripts: 80.4% when the issue contains reproduction steps, 79.9% partial, 70.1% in natural language, 64% with not enough info. If a tool found one right file, repair success was 82.2% (Learn-by-interact) and 69.6% (W&B Programmer).
limits: Analysis of submitted logs, not a controlled experiment; no matched pipeline-versus-agent contrast; Python only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 9: a correct location does not guarantee a correct fix, and a poor reproduction is a common early error. No hypothesis-revision rate reported.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Coherence Collapse: diagnosing why code agents fail after reaching the right code (TrajEval)
finding: For capable models, most failed SWE-bench runs do not fail at finding the code. They reach and edit the right functions and still submit a wrong patch. This is the nearest published count to 'fail after a good first step', and it argues against a wrong first location as the main cause.
numbers: 16,758 trajectories, 3 agent architectures, 7 models. SWE-Agent on SWE-bench Verified, failures only: Edit-Quality bucket (right functions edited, patch still wrong) GPT-5 68.1% (n=163), GPT-5-mini 69.1%, Qwen3-Coder-480B 66.8%, Qwen3-235B 64.7%; weighted average 56.9% of 1,607 failures. Search-stage failures 19.3% (weighted). Weak Qwen3-8B fails upstream: Search 41.1%. On PolyBench the weighted Search share rises to 47.0%.
quote: 60-69% of failures on SWE-Agent and OpenHands reach and edit the correct functions yet still produce incorrect patches
limits: Buckets use a reference patch and a 0.5 recall threshold; 'edited the right function' says nothing about which hypothesis the agent held. Not coded in the Ko and Myers chain form. Edit-Quality is a residual bucket.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a wrong first location is a minority failure for strong models; the large share is a wrong or lost fix after correct localisation. Schema effort belongs on fix verification (G3), not only on diagnosis (G2).

source: Kim et al. (2026) Coherence Collapse, edit-commit checkpoint and consensus trigger
finding: Some agents write a correct patch mid-run and then destroy it. Freezing an edit that passes the test suite recovers those cases. A trigger built from agreement between other models' file choices (no reference patch) gave a small gain that was not significant.
numbers: Coherence Collapse rate among Edit-Quality failures: 39.7% on SWE-bench (n=914); PolyBench overall 32.3 (Python 26.4, Java 36.3, JS 42.1, TS 32.1). 5 mid-run edits bit-identical to gold; all 5 pass the full test suite when re-run. 30 of 97 Near-Correct-Corrupted cases reconstruct gold hunks (exact or near). GPT-5 re-run on 500 instances: baseline 66.0% (330), oracle trigger 70.6% (+4.6, p<.001), consensus-of-3 trigger 69.0% (+3.0, McNemar p=0.08); 39 instances gained, 24 lost; consensus precision 52.4%.
limits: Checkpointing shown on only 5 cases (existence proof, not a measured gain). Consensus result is sub-threshold at alpha 0.05, one model, one harness. Token cost not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a cheap trigger that is not an LLM log reader (test pass, then freeze the edit) can protect a good state. Rollback to an earlier good state is supported as a mechanism; the measured gain is +3.0 points with about coin-flip precision.

source: Liu et al. (2025) An empirical study on failures in automated issue solving (SWE-Bench Verified)
finding: Manual coding of 150 failed instances gave 3 phases, 9 categories, 25 subcategories. Agent tools (OpenHands) fail mostly late, by looping on a failed strategy. Pipeline tools (Agentless) fail early, by wrong localisation. Coders traced about 65% of failures to flawed reasoning, including fixating on issue keywords and not changing strategy.
numbers: 500 instances: OpenHands 53.0% (265), Agentless 50.8% (254), Tools+Claude 49.0%. Causes: flawed reasoning about 65%, knowledge deficiency about 25%, environmental friction about 10%. Runs failing from flawed reasoning took on average 3.5 times more interaction steps than successes. OpenHands: 80% of successes done within 25 rounds, 80% of failures need 54. Localisation share of failures on Easy tasks 41% (OpenHands), 39% (Tools+Claude). Pairwise kappa 0.72-0.77. Expert-Executor (a supervising agent that reviews the plan) resolved 24 of 108 issues OpenHands had failed (22.2%).
limits: One backbone family (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), Python only, 150 hand-coded failures; cause shares are approximate in the text. The Expert-Executor test is on previously failed issues, so regression to the mean may inflate it. No equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 4: fixation on a failing strategy is a coded, common agent failure; an external plan review broke some deadlocks. Token cost was not controlled, so a 'change the hypothesis' rule is supported in direction only.

source: Barke et al. (2026) AgentRx: diagnosing AI agent failures from execution trajectories
finding: Checking each step against constraints built from tool schemas and policies, then giving the violation log to an LLM judge, finds the first unrecoverable step much better than a log-reading LLM alone. This is a trigger that is not a plain transcript read.
numbers: 170 annotated trajectories, 11 settings (v2). Critical-step accuracy, Who&When-style judge vs AgentRx (mean of 3 runs): tau-bench 18.8 vs 42.7; Magentic-One 22.7 vs 36.4; RelWork 32.6 vs 61.5. Ablation on tau-bench step-index accuracy: judge alone 29.9, plus violation log 42.7 (step-by-step constraint generation), 41.0 (one-shot); mean step distance 5.4 falls to 3.8. Category accuracy 47% on tau-bench. Abstract: step localisation up 75% on average over prior work.
limits: Not code-agent tasks (tau-bench, web/file, incident management). Its 'critical step' definition differs from Who&When (the paper shows Who&When can mark a step the agent recovered from). GPT-5 judge; absolute accuracy under 50% on tau-bench. An earlier version reported 115 trajectories; v2 reports 170.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: rule-based violations lift step localisation by about 13 points over the judge alone, yet absolute accuracy stays under 50% on the hardest set. Use checks (test, schema, diff) as the trigger and the LLM only to explain.

source: Ma et al. (2026) DoVer: intervention-driven auto debugging for LLM multi-agent systems
finding: Testing a failure hypothesis by editing a message or plan and re-running turned many failed runs into successes. The authors also found that several different single-step interventions can each fix one failed task, so naming 'the' error step is often ill-posed.
numbers: Magentic-One on GAIA and AssistantBench derived sets: 18-28% of failed trials flipped to success, up to 16% milestone progress, 30-60% of failure hypotheses validated or refuted. GSMPlus with AG2: 49% of failed trials recovered. Abstract and introduction values; per-dataset table not re-read.
quote: log-only debugging lacks validation, producing untested hypotheses
limits: Multi-agent web tasks, not code. Counts failures flipped on re-run with an edit, so some flips may be sampling luck; no pure-resampling control seen in the part read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 2: supports 'test a hypothesis by an intervention, not by reading the log'. Also warns that a single decisive-step label may not exist, which weakens a rule to roll back to the earliest critical step.

source: Huang et al. (2026) TraceCoder: trace-driven multi-agent debugging of LLM-generated code (ICSE 2026)
finding: In a repair loop, adding instrumented runtime traces (variable state) mattered more than the rollback and lesson-memory parts. Dropping the iterative repair loop hurt most.
numbers: BigCodeBench-Complete Pass@1: full 89.04; without instrumentation 78.51 (-10.5); without instrumentation and analysis 75.09; without iterative repair 53.77; without rollback 84.55 (-4.5); without historical-lesson memory 86.75; without both 84.43. Abstract: up to 34.43% relative Pass@1 gain over baselines; iterative repair alone 65.61% relative gain.
limits: Method paper: ablations remove whole multi-agent components, so 'trace vs error message' is confounded with extra LLM calls. Tokens not matched in the ablation read. One benchmark table read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 5: variable-state signal gives the largest single drop when removed (-10.5), above rollback (-4.5). Supports signal richness over pass/fail, consistent with LDB (K09), but it is not a clean controlled comparison.

source: Arimbur (2026) How many tries does it take? Iterative self-repair across model scales and benchmarks
finding: Feeding back the raw error message lifts pass rate for all seven modern models, even 8B. Repair success depends on error type: logic (assertion) failures are the hardest. Most of the gain comes in the first two rounds.
numbers: 7 models, HumanEval (164) and MBPP Sanitized (257), up to 5 attempts, greedy decoding. Gains +4.9 to +17.1 pp (HumanEval), +16.0 to +30.0 pp (MBPP). Best final pass: Gemini 2.5 Flash 96.3% HumanEval, 93.8% MBPP. Name errors repaired about 77%, assertion errors about 45%. Two rounds capture 76-95% of achievable gain. Chain-of-thought repair prompt gives +5.5 pp extra repair gain over a minimal prompt (Llama 3.3 70B). Self-repair matches or beats independent resampling in tokens for all models except the 8B.
limits: Single independent author, free-tier APIs, greedy decoding, small easy benchmarks, one run per setting (paper notes session-level variance). Compares only raw error text, not pass/fail or traces.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 8: a cheap signal (the error message) already works for slips; the 45% vs 77% split mirrors K10/K11 (logic bugs resist feedback). Newer models reverse the old 'weak models are hurt by self-repair' finding of Olausson.

source: Kim (2026) Inducing code change in LLM self-debugging: effects on program repair (AI 7(10):392)
finding: Seen only as an abstract through a search summary (the full page returned 403). Reports that many revise requests return unchanged code, that a 'the code must change' instruction raises structural change, and that giving the first reported failure instead of only pass/fail status raises repair most.
numbers: 9,790 Python programs from 6 open-weight models, 3 benchmarks; 4,168 initially failed; revision requests changed about 57% of failing programs and repaired about 16%. Change instruction: +7.9 to +31.9 points structural change, +0.8 to +1.9 points repair. First reported failure vs status only: +12.9 to +13.4 points across 4 settings (largest effect). Provisional: from the abstract summary only.
limits: Abstract only; not opened in full. Models and benchmarks not verified.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 4: the nearest published direct comparison of pass/fail against the failing message (+13 points), and a sign that forcing a changed attempt helps only a little (+1-2 points). No human-feedback comparison.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? (ISSTA)
finding: A ranked list of suspicious statements helped only on the easy task. Programmers who clicked the faulty line mostly did not recognise it. Some programmers stopped the failure without fixing the fault. Human evidence that seeing the symptom or the fault line is not understanding the defect.
numbers: 34 students; main experiment 24 (groups A, B), follow-up 10 (groups C, D). Tetris mean 12:42 (tool) vs 14:14 (no tool), significant; NanoXML no effect. Completions: 18 Tetris vs 10 NanoXML. Of 10 who clicked the fault line, only 1 stopped; the rest spent about 10 more minutes (61% of their time) in the tool. 37% of list visits jumped more than one position, mean skip 10, mean 10.3 zigzags. Moving the fault from rank 7 to 35 (Tetris) or 83 to 16 (NanoXML) changed nothing significant.
limits: Small N, students, two tasks. A study of a localisation tool, not a replication of the Ko and Myers shares; it does not code breakdown types.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (partial): the Ko and Myers shares were not tested here. It does support G3: a vanished symptom or a located line is not proof that the defect is understood or fixed (cf. K15).

source: Samir and Rahman (2026) Improved bug localization with AI agents leveraging hypothesis and dynamic cognition (CogniGent, ICPC 2026)
finding: A multi-agent localiser that forms several root-cause hypotheses from the bug report and tests them with call-graph analysis beat six baselines on bug localisation. It tests localisation only, not end-to-end repair, and the hypothesis step is not ablated on its own in the part read.
numbers: 591 bug reports; MAP improvement 23.33-38.57% (document and method levels); MRR improvement 25.14-53.74%; significance tests reported. Abstract and introduction read; the ablation table was not read.
limits: Localisation, not repair; relative gains over IR-style and LLM baselines; no equal-token control seen; hypothesis-first is bundled with call-graph and context engineering.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: nearest published support for 'several hypotheses plus a test'. Not a controlled ablation of three rival hypotheses before the first edit; the gap stays open.

source: Gap search log, 2026-10-31: searches that found nothing
finding: No published study was found for: (a) forcing 3 rival hypotheses with cheap tests before the first edit at equal tokens, with a logic-vs-syntax split; (b) a Whyline-style 'state the assumption behind each why question' prompt for an LLM; (c) token-level surprise as a slip flag with a false-alarm rate on agent plans; (d) agent failures coded in the Ko and Myers root-breakdown-then-error form; (e) a later human study that re-measures the Ko and Myers skill/rule/knowledge shares. Web-search quota ran out partway and the arXiv and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited, so these mean not found in the searches run, not proof of absence.
numbers: Web searches that returned results: 6. Refused after quota: 2 or more. Papers opened in full text this pass: d16-d22, d24, d25.
limits: Absence claims are weak because of the search limits. Reason (1990), Gilmore, Vessey and Katz and Anderson were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 7, 9, 10 stay open; write them as untested hypotheses in the schema notes, not as findings.
